name: Zygomatic reduction
lead: Zygomatic reduction, also called reduction malarplasty, cheekbone reduction or cheekbone shaving, is surgery that narrows the cheekbones or lowers their projection, giving a slimmer, more oval facial outline.[1][2] People pursue it to reduce a wide midface, soften prominent cheek angles and balance the face against the jaw and forehead.[3] Because the zygomatic bones set the width of the face at cheek level, changing them changes the face's overall shape from the front.[10]

The operation is most associated with East Asia, where an oval or 'melon seed' face is considered delicate and attractive and cosmetic bone contouring has become increasingly popular; requests have also been rising in the United States.[1][3] One surgeon's report describes reduction malarplasty as the most common facial-contouring operation in Asian countries and says prominent zygomas are perceived by many Asian patients as unattractive.[20] The standard modern technique is an L-shaped osteotomy in which the zygomatic body and arch are cut, repositioned inward and fixed with screws, usually through incisions inside the mouth and a small incision by the sideburn.[6]

Published work is mainly surgical technique series and reviews. A 2023 meta-analysis pooled 29 studies and 6,611 patients to compare complications among reduction malarplasty methods.[4] In looksmaxxing forums the procedure is discussed in relation to face width, the eye-spacing ratio (ESR) and facial harmony, with before-and-after examples cited on both sides.[8][9][16]

chain: Cheekbone is cut, repositioned or shaved
Midface width and cheek projection decrease
angle.text: The procedure changes the bony frame under the cheeks, reducing bizygomatic width or forward projection so the face reads narrower and softer. People with a wide or angular midface use it to move toward an oval contour.

paras: The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone and part of the lateral and inferior wall of the eye socket; its temporal process joins the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch, and the masseter muscle attaches to its lower border.[10] A review of skeletal contouring in ethnic patients states that the zygomaticomaxillary complex and mandible shape how overlying soft tissue is draped and lit, that their size and projection are sexually dimorphic and ethnically defined, and that excessive projection in any dimension can look undesirable to some patients.[3]

Aesthetic ideals vary: a cosmetic bone contouring review notes that in some cultures a wide jaw and square face are considered less attractive while an oval face is viewed as feminine and delicate.[1] Wikipedia notes that, in other cultures, high cheekbones are considered attractive and cheek augmentation is a cosmetic option, so the same bone can be a target for reduction or augmentation depending on the ideal.[10]

Surgeons distinguish a prominent zygomatic body (cheek projection) from a wide arch (width). The 2023 meta-analysis states that the L-shaped osteotomy gives a better effect when both body and arch protrude.[4] Reviews list reduction malarplasty together with mandibular angle and lateral cortex reduction and genioplasty as a family of facial skeleton procedures.[1]

Reduction malarplasty has been described in the plastic surgery literature since at least the early 1990s in the sources listed here, and a 2015 technical report cites a 1983 report as an earlier description.[11][12][20] Its author, a Seoul practitioner, cites later contributions including an intraoral approach from 2000 and a 2009 retrospective series of 418 cases using an intraoral L-shaped osteotomy.[20]

One L-shaped osteotomy technique through intraoral and sideburn incisions removes a middle segment of the anterior zygomatic body, fractures the arch root through a small incision, and repositions the freed complex medially with one or two screws; a series of 32 patients reported simple manipulation, stable fixation and less risk of a drooping face.[6] Another published variant, the rotation technique, removes no bone and instead rotates the most prominent point of the zygomaticomaxillary complex medially, contouring the posterior maxillary sinus wall to close the gap and fixing the segment with plates and screws; it is reported with photographs of two patients.[20]

Newer work describes digital planning, augmented reality and robot-assisted techniques in facial bone contouring, and an intraoral skeletal contouring simulator for surgeon training; the authors of the 2023 review say digital planning can shorten operative time and reduce bleeding.[5][7] A three-dimensional CT study of 80 patients after L-shaped malarplasty found that bone setback or resection correlated with changes in anterior and middle zygomatic width and protrusion, and the authors proposed a regression equation to help preoperative planning.[13]

The 2023 meta-analysis found that L-shaped osteotomy without bony resection had the lowest postoperative complication incidence (0.02%) but limits how much bone can be removed; with larger resections, long-arm and short-arm resection variants were each preferable depending on whether structural or functional complications were weighed.[4] A correction to the paper was later published.[19]

The Seoul surgeon's report names nonunion or malunion and drooping of the cheek as the two most common complications, and links nonunion to the masseter's attachment to the zygoma, arguing for rigid fixation and close bone contact.[20][10] Case reports describe maxillary sinusitis after the operation, including two cases treated with endoscopic sinus surgery.[14]

Because blood supply to the maxillofacial area is abundant and the intraoral field is narrow, hemostasis is a recognised challenge in facial contouring surgery; a randomized study of 282 patients across four contouring procedures evaluated a soluble hemostatic gauze.[15] Reviews advise that surgeons offering contouring operations be familiar with their potential complications.[1]

On looksmax.org the topic is raised mainly by people with wide faces. A poster asks whether cheekbone shaving could improve a ratio of 0.43 by narrowing the face and whether his zygomas are too narrow to qualify; replies include that the ratio is 'overrated' and that brow position matters more for harmony.[9] Another thread asks whether cheekbone shaving can fix a low ESR, with one poster arguing that shaving does little and that cutting a segment of the zygomatic arch and rejoining the ends is what reduces width; another reply suggests a longer face vertically is what is needed.[16]

A longer thread discusses wide skulls and 'bloated' faces, distinguishing fat from bone as the cause of width. The poster says buccal fat removal is often a poor decision because it can lead to an aged look, and says a slimmer face is generally better, citing malarplasty, 'shaving' and reduction as one and the same operation; another remark in the thread says shaving reduces forward projection more than width.[8] The thread contrasts an example described as very good with a public figure said to have lost his strengths after cheekbone and mandible work, and a reply says surgery should follow genuine need and warns of 'not knowing your face'.[8]
A further thread, titled around a 'ZSO malarplasty', asks whether the poster needs the procedure.[17]

Surgical reviews present reduction malarplasty and mandibuloplasty as techniques that can reshape the facial skeleton toward a desired shape, within the cultural framing of the patient's ideal.[3] The cosmetic bone contouring review states that these procedures 'may be performed to alter the facial contour and bring about dramatic results', and that surgeons should know the potential complications.[1]
No study found compares looksmaxxing-style ratios, such as ESR, before and after cheekbone surgery, and no randomized trial comparing surgery with no surgery on appearance was identified.

Evidence consists of surgical technique reports, reviews and observational series. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies (6,611 patients, literature from 1983 to early 2022) compared complications across reduction malarplasty methods.[4] A retrospective 3D CT study of 80 patients measured zygomatic width and protrusion changes after L-shaped malarplasty.[13] A 32-patient technique series reported outcomes of one L-shaped osteotomy approach.[6] A randomized study of 282 patients examined a hemostatic gauze across four facial contouring procedures,[15] and a randomized study evaluated a surgical training simulator for intraoral contouring operations.[7] No randomized trial comparing surgery with no surgery on appearance was identified.

lore.intro: Forum members discuss cheekbone shaving mainly for wide faces and as a way to change facial ratios, and they trade before-and-after examples.[8][9]

claims.claim: Cheekbone shaving mainly reduces forward projection, not width.
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster says shaving primarily reduces forward cheekbone projection, and that cheekbone reduction by cutting the arch is the way to narrow the face.[8][16]
claims.experts: Surgical literature describes reduction malarplasty as cutting and repositioning the zygomatic body and arch to reduce width and protrusion, with measured changes in width after L-shaped osteotomy.[6][13]

claims.claim: It can ascend a wide face but can harm a well-proportioned one.
claims.believers: A poster contrasts a wide-faced example with a good result and a celebrity example said to have lost features after cheekbone and mandible work; another reply says surgery should follow genuine need.[8]
claims.experts: Reviews note that procedures can bring dramatic contour changes and require familiarity with potential complications.[1]

claims.claim: Cheekbone surgery can raise the eye-to-eye spacing ratio (ESR).
claims.believers: Posters argue narrowing the zygomatic arch makes the face less wide and increases ESR, while others say a longer face rather than a shorter one is needed or that ESR is overrated.[9][16]
claims.experts: No published studies were identified linking malarplasty to eye-spacing ratios.

claims.claim: A wide face may be bone or fat, and the cause matters for the choice of procedure.
claims.believers: A poster says width can come from fat or bone and that buccal fat removal can age the face, so bone reduction suits some wide faces.[8]
claims.experts: Skeletal contouring reviews describe zygomaticomaxillary projection as ethnically defined and shaping the overlying soft tissue, which is the basis for choosing between bone and soft-tissue approaches.[3]

claims.claim: The arch cut and reposition technique narrows the face with low complication rates.
claims.believers: Posters describe cutting a piece of the arch and joining the ends as the way to make the face less wide.[16]
claims.experts: A 2023 meta-analysis found L-shaped osteotomy without resection had the lowest complication incidence (0.02%) but limits the amount of bone removed; a surgeon's report names nonunion and cheek drooping as the main complications.[4][20]

claims.claim: Cheekbone reduction in Korea or other Asian centres is the destination for this surgery.
claims.believers: A poster asks whether cheekbone shaving could be done in Korea to improve his ratio.[9]
claims.experts: Reviews describe reduction malarplasty as most popular in East Asia, with growing requests in the United States.[1][3]

card.summary: Surgery to narrow or flatten the cheekbones; popular in Asian aesthetic surgery, with no outcome studies available.
card.note: Forum members themselves report mixed before-and-after outcomes; no studies found.

quick.overview:
Zygomatic reduction is a surgery that reshapes or repositions the cheekbones to make the face narrower. It is also called malarplasty or cheekbone shaving.
On looksmax.org, users with wide faces discuss it and argue over whether it helps or ruins proportions. No studies were found for this wiki entry.
quick.mechanism: The bone of the cheek is cut and reshaped or repositioned inward, as forum posters describe it. Some say shaving mainly reduces forward projection rather than width.
quick.risks: Forum users describe results ranging from very good to very bad. It is a bone-cutting operation under anaesthesia; complication data are limited.
